PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND CLINICAL ASPECTS

In brief: Digestive health is not merely the absence of disease, but a dynamic balance between protective factors (mucosa, enzymes, flora) and aggressive factors (acids, toxins, pathogens). Understanding pathological mechanisms is essential for precise diagnosis and targeted therapy.

GASTRODUODENAL ULCER: THE IMBALANCE

An ulcer is a lesion penetrating beyond the mucosa into the submucosa and often the muscularis. It results from the disruption of epithelial physiological balance:

Aggressive Factors
Chemical & Bacterial Insults
Hydrochloric acid (HCl), pepsin, Helicobacter pylori infection (urease activity/toxins), and NSAIDs.
Protective Factors
Mucosal Barrier Defenses
Mucin layer, Bicarbonate secretion (HCO₃⁻), adequate blood microcirculation, and Prostaglandins E₂.
▼
Clinical Picture
Epithelial Damage & Symptomatic Presentation
Postprandial epigastric pain (early in gastric ulcers, late/relieved by food in duodenal ulcers), nausea, and risk of complications (hemorrhage, perforation).

Helicobacter pylori is a microaerophilic Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the gastric mucosa. By producing urease, it converts urea into ammonia and CO₂, neutralizing local acid to survive and releasing cytotoxins (VacA, CagA) that damage epithelial cells.

MALABSORPTION: WHEN ABSORPTION FAILS

Malabsorption defines the reduced ability of the small intestine to assimilate nutrients, electrolytes, or vitamins. The primary etiopathogeneses include:

  • Enzyme and digestive deficiencies: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, lactase deficiency.
  • Structural mucosal damage: Villous atrophy in celiac disease, transmural inflammation in Crohn's disease, radiation therapy effects.
  • Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO): Abnormal proliferation in the small intestine competing for nutrients (e.g., vitamin B12).
  • Reduced absorptive surface: Short bowel syndrome from surgical resection.

Key symptoms include steatorrhea (evacuation of undigested fats), weight loss, iron-deficiency or megaloblastic anemia, osteopenia from Vitamin D/Calcium deficiency, and abdominal bloating.

IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME (IBS)

IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder with a multifactorial etiology, lacking structural lesions detectable by conventional imaging. Pathogenesis includes:

  • Visceral hypersensitivity: Lowered pain threshold to mechanical and distension stimuli.
  • Intestinal dysmotility: Altered peristaltic waves (hyper/hypomotility).
  • Quantitative and qualitative dysbiosis: Alteration of the indigenous microbiome.
  • Gut-Brain Axis dysregulation: Psychosocial modulation and altered responses to stress.

Diagnosis is based on the Rome IV Criteria and is a diagnosis of exclusion of organic diseases (IBD, celiac disease, neoplasms).

DIGESTIVE NEOPLASMS: COLON AND STOMACH CANCER

Malignant tumors of the digestive tract represent a primary share of oncological pathology. Most colorectal carcinomas originate from adenomatous polyps through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (accumulation of mutations in APC, KRAS, p53).

Risk factors include advanced age, diets high in red/processed meats and low fiber, obesity, smoking, and hereditary syndromes (Lynch, FAP).

Symptoms (often late) include change in bowel habits, hematochezia or melena, insidious microcytic anemia, and weight loss. Screening (FOBT and colonoscopy with preventive polypectomy) drastically reduces mortality.

Gastric carcinoma is associated with chronic atrophic gastritis from H. pylori, consumption of salted/smoked foods, and nitrosamines. Diagnosis is often delayed due to non-specific early symptoms (mild dyspepsia).

DIAGNOSTICS: TOOLS AND APPROACHES

The diagnosis of digestive diseases utilizes:

Diagnostic Modality Methodology / Target Clinical Applications & Findings
Blood & Stool Tests Systemic biomarkers Evaluation of anemia (Hb, ferritin), inflammation (CRP, ESR), pancreatic enzymes (amylase/lipase), and FOBT.
Digestive Endoscopy EGD & Colonoscopy Direct mucosal inspection, histological biopsy sampling, and therapeutic procedures (polypectomy).
Diagnostic Imaging US, CT, MRI, MRCP Neoplastic staging, intestinal wall examination, and mapping of the biliary-pancreatic tree.
Functional & Breath Tests Labeled substrates (e.g., ¹³C-Urea, Lactose) Non-invasive diagnosis of H. pylori infection, carbohydrate malabsorption, and SIBO.

MICROBIOTA AND THE GUT-BRAIN AXIS

In brief: The intestine is not just a digestive organ, but a complex ecosystem and a neural processing center. The gut microbiota (the community of microorganisms inhabiting it) constantly communicates with the brain through neural, hormonal, and immune pathways, influencing mood, behavior, and overall health.

THE GUT MICROBIOTA: A SYMBIOTIC ORGANISM

The gut microbiota consists of trillions of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and archaea, with a genetic pool (metagenome) that exceeds the human genome by 150 times. It is not merely a "guest", but a true acquired metabolic organ.

Its main physiological functions include:

  • Digestion of indigestible substrates: Breakdown of fibers and resistant starches producing short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate, propionate, and acetate, essential for colonic mucosal health.
  • Synthesis of essential micronutrients: Biosynthesis of vitamin K, vitamin B12, folates, and biotin.
  • Barrier effect and pathogen protection: Competition for ecological niches, secretion of bacteriocins, and maintenance of tight junction integrity.
  • Immune system modulation: Regulation and development of GALT (up to 70% of the body's lymphoid tissue resides in the gut).

Dysbiosis (qualitative and quantitative alteration of the microbiota) compromises this equilibrium, linking to inflammatory (IBD, IBS), dysmetabolic (obesity, type 2 diabetes), allergic, and neuropsychiatric disorders.

THE GUT-BRAIN AXIS: A CONSTANT DIALOGUE

The gut-brain axis represents a bidirectional communication network connecting the Enteric Nervous System (ENS) to the Central Nervous System (CNS). This dialogue unfolds along four main pathways:

Pathway 1 · Neural
Vagus Nerve and ENS
Primary neural highway for rapid transmission of afferent signals from the intestinal epithelium to the brainstem and vice versa.
Pathway 2 · Endocrine
Enteroendocrine Cells
Secretion of systemic peptides and hormones (e.g., serotonin, ghrelin, leptin) regulating appetite, mood, and stress response.
Pathway 3 · Immune
Cytokines and GALT
Inflammatory mediators produced locally in the gut can cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB), influencing brain function.
Pathway 4 · Metabolic
Microbial Metabolites
SCFAs (butyrate), neurotransmitters, and tryptophan derivatives entering the bloodstream to act directly on central receptors.

NEUROTRANSMITTERS AND MICROBIOTA

The gut microbiota operates as an advanced neurochemical hub, directly producing or modulating the synthesis of key neuromediators:

Neurotransmitter Microbial Origin / Mechanism Physiological Role & Clinical Impact
Serotonin (5-HT) ~90% produced by enterochromaffin cells stimulated by bacterial metabolites. Regulation of gut motility, mood, sleep, and appetite. Alterations linked to anxiety and depression.
GABA (γ-aminobutyrate) Synthesized directly by strains such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium. Primary central inhibitory neurotransmitter; exerts anxiolytic and relaxing effects.
Dopamine Synthesis and tissue modulation driven by specific microbial populations. Regulation of reward circuits, motivation, and motor coordination.
Acetylcholine Produced by several commensal bacterial strains within the enteric environment. Modulation of memory, cognitive functions, and visceral smooth muscle contraction.

Scientific evidence underscores how targeted modulation of the microbiota (via probiotics, prebiotics, or fecal microbiota transplantation FMT) represents a new therapeutic frontier in psychiatry and neurology.

IMMUNITY AND MICROBIOTA

The microbiota is essential for the development and homeostasis of the immune system. By interacting with mucosal immune cells (T lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells), it maintains a constant balance between immunological tolerance (towards food antigens and commensals) and defensive response (against pathogens).

Early dysbiosis during the first years of life can alter immune maturation, predisposing to autoimmune diseases, allergies, and asthma. SCFAs (particularly butyrate) exert potent anti-inflammatory effects and strengthen the intestinal barrier, preventing hyperpermeability ("leaky gut").

KEY FACTORS SHAPING MICROBIAL COMPOSITION

The structure and diversity of the gut microbial ecosystem are shaped by four key factors:

Nutrition
Diet and Nutrients
Diets rich in fibers and fermented foods promote bacterial biodiversity; saturated fats and refined sugars foster dysbiosis.
Pharmacology
Pharmacological Treatments
Antibiotics cause drastic alterations to the microbiome; PPIs, NSAIDs, and psychotropic drugs also impact its composition.
Lifestyle
Stress and Environment
Chronic stress, sleep deprivation, and sedentary habits alter gut motility and mucosal barrier function.
Early Development
Birth and Breastfeeding
Vaginal delivery and breastfeeding foster colonization by a more diverse and beneficial microflora.

Maintaining gut microbiota eubiosis is a fundamental pillar for overall health, from the gut to the brain.

BIOCHEMICAL DEEP DIVE

In brief: Digestion is not limited to mechanical breakdown but is the starting point for complex metabolic pathways. Understanding enzyme kinetics, the Krebs Cycle (the cell's energy engine), and the Urea Cycle (the nitrogen disposal system) is fundamental to understanding how nutrients are converted into energy and biomolecules, and how the body manages toxic waste products.

ENZYME KINETICS: THE MICHAELIS-MENTEN EQUATION

The rate at which an enzyme catalyzes a reaction is not linear with substrate concentration but follows a hyperbolic curve described by the Michaelis-Menten equation. This model describes the relationship between reaction velocity (V) and substrate concentration ([S]).

The fundamental equation is:

V = Vmax [S] Km + [S]

Where:

  • Vmax is the theoretical maximum reaction velocity, reached when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate.
  • Km (Michaelis Constant) is the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half of Vmax. It is an inverse index of the enzyme's affinity for the substrate: a low Km indicates high affinity (the enzyme works efficiently even at low substrate concentrations), while a high Km indicates low affinity.

Michaelis-Menten kinetics are fundamental for understanding metabolic regulation and pharmacodynamics. Enzyme inhibitors alter kinetic parameters in characteristic ways:

Inhibition Type Effect on Vmax Effect on Km Mechanism of Action
Competitive Unchanged Increases (apparent) Inhibitor binds to the free active site. Overcome by increasing [S].
Non-Competitive Decreases Unchanged Inhibitor binds to an allosteric site on both free enzyme and ES complex.
Uncompetitive Decreases Decreases (apparent) Inhibitor binds exclusively to the Enzyme-Substrate (ES) complex.

THE KREBS CYCLE (TRICARBOXYLIC ACID CYCLE)

The Krebs Cycle, located in the mitochondrial matrix, is the central metabolic pathway for the complete oxidation of nutrients. It is the convergence point for the catabolism of carbohydrates, lipids, and amino acids, and the primary source of reducing power (NADH, FADH2) for the respiratory chain.

Initial Phase · Step 1
Condensation & Citrate Synthesis
Acetyl-CoA (2C) condenses with Oxaloacetate (4C) to form Citrate (6C). Irreversible and strongly exergonic reaction catalyzed by citrate synthase.
↓
Oxidative Phase · Steps 2 - 4
Isomerization & Oxidative Decarboxylation
Citrate is converted to Isocitrate and undergoes two successive oxidative decarboxylations (via isocitrate DH and α-ketoglutarate DH), releasing 2 CO2 and generating 2 NADH + Succinyl-CoA (4C).
↓
Energetic Phase · Step 5
Substrate-Level Phosphorylation
Cleavage of the high-energy thioester bond of Succinyl-CoA (via succinyl-CoA synthetase) is coupled to direct synthesis of 1 GTP / ATP and formation of Succinate.
↓
Regeneration Phase · Steps 6 - 8
Dehydrogenation & Oxaloacetate Regeneration
Succinate is oxidized to Fumarate (generating 1 FADH2 via succinate DH), hydrated to L-Malate, and finally oxidized to Oxaloacetate (generating 1 NADH via malate DH), restarting the cycle.

Net yield per oxidized Acetyl-CoA molecule:

  • 3 NADH (transfer 6 high-energy electrons to the respiratory chain).
  • 1 FADH2 (electron donor to mitochondrial Complex II).
  • 1 GTP / ATP (generated via substrate-level phosphorylation by succinyl-CoA synthetase).
  • 2 CO2 (waste byproducts of oxidative decarboxylation).

The Krebs Cycle is an amphibolic pathway (both catabolic and anabolic): it provides intermediates for gluconeogenesis, fatty acid synthesis, amino acids, and porphyrins. It is allosterically regulated by energy charge (ATP/ADP) and redox state (NADH/NAD+).

THE UREA CYCLE: NITROGEN DISPOSAL

Amino acid catabolism releases amino groups (-NH2) as ammonia (NH3/NH4+), which is neurotoxic at micromolar levels. The liver converts ammonia into urea via a metabolic cycle requiring spatial coordination between the mitochondrion and cytosol.

Mitochondrial Phase · Step 1
Carbamoyl Phosphate Formation
NH4+ + HCO3- + 2 ATP → Carbamoyl Phosphate + 2 ADP + Pi. Catalyzed by Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS I), allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate.
↓
Mitochondrial Phase · Step 2
Citrulline Synthesis & Cytosolic Transport
Carbamoyl Phosphate reacts with Ornithine (via Ornithine Transcarbamylase - OTC) forming Citrulline, which is translocated to the cytosol.
↓
Cytosolic Phase · Steps 3 & 4
Condensation & Argininosuccinate Cleavage
Citrulline binds to Aspartate (donating the second amino group) consuming 1 ATP → AMP + PPi (2 high-energy bonds). Argininosuccinate is then cleaved into Arginine and Fumarate (Krebs link).
↓
Cytosolic / Final Phase · Step 5
Arginine Hydrolysis & Ornithine Regeneration
Arginase cleaves Arginine, releasing Urea (for renal excretion) and regenerating Ornithine, which re-enters the mitochondrion.

The cycle consumes the stoichiometric equivalent of 4 high-energy phosphate bonds (3 ATP → 2 ADP + 1 AMP) per molecule of urea produced. Genetic defects in urea cycle enzymes (e.g., OTC deficiency) cause severe hyperammonemia, requiring protein restriction and alternative nitrogen scavengers.

METABOLIC INTEGRATION: ENERGY FLOW

These three systems operate in tight metabolic coordination:

  • Fumarate produced in the urea cycle directly enters the mitochondrion to feed the Krebs Cycle (Krebs-urea bicycle).
  • ATP generated by the respiratory chain via Krebs/NADH drives the energetic cost of the urea cycle and hepatic biosynthesis.
  • Enzyme kinetic parameters (Km and Vmax) govern the liver's metabolic flexibility when shifting between postprandial and fasted states.

Understanding these interconnections is vital for clinical biochemistry, laying the groundwork to diagnose inherited metabolic disorders, hepatic encephalopathy, and evaluate nutritional status.

DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Introduction to digestion

Humans need to eat in order to:

  • Grow.
  • Replace damaged cells.
  • Recover the energy used by various organs.

The first step is called nutrition: it is when we eat food.

Food cannot be used immediately by the body. It must be transformed. This process is called digestion. Digestion takes place in the digestive system.

During this process, special organs (glands) release chemicals. These substances help break food down into smaller pieces.

Digestion is therefore a process that simplifies food until it can be absorbed by the body.
en.digestive_simple:
DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

Introduction to Digestion

Humans need to eat to:

  • Grow.
  • Replace cells that break down.
  • Regain the energy used by various organs.

The first step is called feeding: it is when we eat food.

Food cannot be used immediately by the body. It must be transformed. This process is called digestion. Digestion takes place in the digestive system.

During this process, special organs (glands) release chemical substances. These substances help break food down into smaller pieces.

Digestion is therefore a process that simplifies food until it can be absorbed by the body.

The Digestive System

The digestive system is like a long tube running from the mouth to the anus. It is made up of several sections, each with a different shape, length, and function.

The Main Sections

  • Mouth: it is the entry point for food. It is closed by the lips in front and connected to the pharynx behind.
  • Pharynx: the meeting point for food and air. Food passes into the esophagus, air into the lungs.
  • Esophagus: a tube connecting the pharynx to the stomach.
  • Stomach: the widest part of the tube. It has a shape similar to a bagpipe, which varies depending on the individual.
  • Intestine: follows the stomach. It is divided into two parts: small and large.

The Small Intestine

It is about 6 meters and 80 centimeters long. It has three parts:

  • Duodenum: juices from the liver and pancreas arrive here to help digest food.
  • Jejunum
  • Ileum: the final part of the small intestine, which connects to the large intestine.

The Large Intestine

It is about 1 meter and 80 centimeters long. It has the following parts:

  • Cecum: the beginning of the large intestine. The ileum connects here via a valve: the ileocecal valve.
  • Ascending colon: goes up the right side of the abdomen.
  • Transverse colon: runs from right to left, below the liver.
  • Descending colon: goes down the left side.
  • Rectum: the final part, where feces accumulate.
  • Anal sphincter: a muscle that opens and closes the anus, allowing feces to be expelled.

The Internal Surface of the Intestine

Inside, the intestine has a special mucosa. In the small intestine, there are:

  • Circular folds (Valvulae conniventes): folds of the mucosa that increase the surface area.
  • Intestinal villi: small projections that absorb nutrients from food.

They are like tiny hairs that capture digested sugars, proteins, and fats.

Function of the Large Intestine

The large intestine digests very little, but it plays an important role thanks to the bacteria living inside it (intestinal flora).

These microorganisms:

  • Help produce certain vitamins (such as vitamin K).
  • Digest parts of food that the rest of the intestine cannot process.

Although useful, too many or the wrong kinds of bacteria can cause illness. For this reason, medically speaking, the large intestine is studied more for its diseases than for its normal functioning.

Feces

Feces are not just leftover food. They consist of:

  • Undigested food residues (e.g., fiber).
  • Material from the digestive tract (such as dead cells and mucus).
  • Billions of dead intestinal bacteria.

Feces are expelled to the outside through the anus, controlled by the anal sphincter muscle.

Chewing and Swallowing

1. Mastication and Swallowing

Food is broken down by the teeth and sent into the stomach through the esophagus.

Then food reaches the stomach, where it is mixed with gastric juices to become a semi-liquid mass.

Chewing

Chewing is the first step of digestion.

The teeth cut, break, and crush food. The tongue and cheeks move food around the mouth, mixing it with saliva.

This process creates a soft ball called a food bolus. The bolus is easier to swallow.

Jaw movements are controlled by the brain, specifically areas in the medulla oblongata (bulb) and the temporal cortex. The muscles involved are:

  • Masseters
  • Temporalis
  • Pterygoids (internal and external)
  • Jaw depressor muscles

Enzymes: The Little Helpers of Digestion

Enzymes are substances that help transform food. They act like catalysts: they speed up chemical reactions without changing themselves.

Each enzyme works on only one type of food. Examples:

  • Pepsin digests proteins, not fats or sugars.
  • Rennet solidifies milk casein.
  • Maltase breaks down maltose, but not sucrose.

Enzymes can be broken down by heat or toxic substances, but when used properly, they last a long time.

Already in the 1700s, the scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani understood that stomach juices (containing enzymes) transform food.

Salivary Glands and Saliva

Three pairs of glands produce saliva:

  • Parotid glands
  • Sublingual glands
  • Submandibular glands

What Does Saliva Contain?

Saliva is mostly water (98.7%). It also contains organic and inorganic substances.

Inorganic Substances:

  • Chlorides: help the enzyme amylase work.
  • Bicarbonates and phosphates: keep the pH of saliva close to neutral. This is important because enzymes function best in this environment.

Organic Substances:

  • Mucin: makes saliva viscous. It helps lubricate food and the inside of the mouth.
  • Enzymes: the most important is ptyalin.

Ptyalin

Ptyalin attacks the starch present in food.

It breaks it down into small parts called dextrins and maltose.

It works best when:

  • Starch is cooked (e.g., pasta, potatoes).
  • The pH is neutral (as in the mouth).

In the stomach, hydrochloric acid stops the action of ptyalin, so its work ends there.

What Is the Purpose of Saliva?

  • Helps to chew better.
  • Favors the formation of the food bolus.
  • Makes swallowing easier.
  • Mucin lubricates food and protects the esophagus.
  • Aids the sense of taste.
  • Protects teeth from decay.
  • Regulates water balance in the body: thirst is an important signal.

How Is Saliva Produced?

Saliva is produced continuously, but in varying quantities.

More is produced when:

  • There is food in the mouth.
  • Food is dry or has a strong flavor.
  • Food is seen, smelled, or thought about (even just remembering it).

The process is controlled by a nervous reflex.

Here is how it works:

  1. Stimuli in the mouth (touch, taste) activate receptors.
  2. The signal goes to the medulla oblongata (bulb) in the brain.
  3. The medulla sends an order to the salivary glands.
  4. The glands produce more saliva.

Fibers of the parasympathetic nervous system stimulate saliva production, having a stronger effect than sympathetic fibers.

Different Types of Saliva

Salivary glands are shaped like small clusters (like grapes), but they produce different types of saliva:

  • Parotid glands: produce clear, watery saliva rich in ptyalin. They exit near the second upper molar through Stensen's duct.
  • Sublingual glands: produce thick, viscous saliva rich in mucin, but without ptyalin. They have many small ducts (15-30), each with its own opening under the tongue.
  • Submandibular glands: produce mixed saliva containing both ptyalin and mucin. They open on the sides of the lingual frenulum via Wharton's duct.

Thanks to these glands, the mouth stays moist, food is well prepared for the stomach, and digestion can begin correctly.

After chewing, food becomes a soft, uniform mixture called a food bolus.

Swallowing

The bolus passes from the mouth into the pharynx. This passage is called swallowing.

From this moment on, food is no longer under our conscious control. Its movement is automatic, managed by reflexes controlled by the medulla oblongata.

What Happens During Swallowing?

  • The soft palate (velo palatino) lifts, blocking the passage to the nose.
  • The epiglottis lowers, covering the larynx and preventing food from entering the respiratory tract.
  • Breathing stops for a moment: this is swallowing apnea.
  • The bolus enters the esophagus.

Movement in the Esophagus: Peristalsis

The esophagus pushes the bolus toward the stomach through muscular movements.

These movements are called peristalsis. They are slow waves of contraction and relaxation:

  • A section of the esophagus contracts and pushes the bolus forward.
  • The next section relaxes to receive it.
  • Then it contracts in turn, and so on.

Peristalsis begins in the esophagus and continues throughout the digestive tract.

From the Esophagus to the Stomach

The bolus reaches the end of the esophagus, where it meets a muscle called the cardia. It is a sphincter that opens and closes.

The peristaltic wave slows down, the cardiac sphincter relaxes and opens, and the bolus enters the stomach.

Gastric Digestion

2. Gastric Digestion

In the stomach, food is mixed with gastric juices to become a sort of cream.

Subsequently, the partially digested food enters the small intestine, where nutrient separation takes place.

How Long Does Digestion Take in the Stomach?

It depends on the type and quantity of food.

  • Fats slow down digestion.
  • For a normal meal, it takes about 3-4 hours.

During this time, food undergoes two types of transformation:

  • Mechanical: movements of the stomach that mix the food.
  • Chemical: action of gastric juices.

Stomach Movements

The stomach muscles contract in waves: this is peristalsis. These movements:

  • Mix the food thoroughly.
  • Help empty the stomach slowly.

Even when the stomach is empty, it can contract strongly, causing the sensation of hunger.

Structure of the Stomach

The stomach walls have multiple layers. The main ones are:

  • Muscular layer (Tunica muscularis): formed by three layers of fibers:
    • Longitudinal (external)
    • Circular (internal)
    • Oblique (innermost)
  • Mucosal layer (Tunica mucosa): lines the inside of the stomach.

Stomach Glands

The mucosa has many grooves, forming hexagonal areas called gastric areas. At the center of each area are openings where gastric glands empty.

These are millions of tiny tubes that produce gastric juice.

Two Important Types of Cells:

  • Chief cells (Principal cells): produce an inactive substance called pepsinogen.
  • Parietal cells (Oxyntic cells): produce hydrochloric acid.

Gastric Juice

It is a clear liquid consisting of:

  • Hydrochloric acid
  • Pepsin
  • Mucin
  • Intrinsic factor
  • Other minor components

Pepsin

It is the enzyme that digests proteins.

It is not present immediately as an active enzyme; it is first produced as pepsinogen (the inactive form).

In the stomach, hydrochloric acid converts pepsinogen into pepsin.

Once activated, pepsin:

  • Digests proteins by breaking them down into smaller pieces: peptones.
  • Helps convert more pepsinogen into pepsin.

What Is the Purpose of Hydrochloric Acid?

  • Creates an acidic environment: necessary for pepsin to work.
  • Kills many bacteria present in food (antiseptic action).
  • Protects the stomach from infections.
  • Allows the production of the intrinsic factor, essential for vitamin B12 absorption.

Lazzaro Spallanzani already observed that meat immersed in gastric juice decomposes more slowly, demonstrating its anti-putrefactive power.

Rennin (Chymosin)

It is an enzyme present in the gastric juice of infants.

It solidifies milk, turning it into a denser mass.

This serves because:

  • Milk stays in the stomach longer.
  • Pepsin has more time to digest milk proteins.

Other Components of Gastric Juice

  • Gastric lipase: begins digesting fats, but its role is small, especially in adults.
  • Mucin: protects the stomach wall, forming a barrier against hydrochloric acid and pepsin. Without it, the stomach would digest itself.

When Is Gastric Juice Produced?

It is not produced continuously. It begins when:

  • Eating takes place.
  • Food is seen, smelled, or thought about.
  • There is appetite (psychological stimulus).

Two Main Phases:

  1. Cephalic phase: Begins even before eating. Controlled by the vagus nerves. Responds to the sight, smell, and thought of food.
  2. Gastric phase: Begins when food enters the stomach. The pyloric mucosa releases a hormone: gastrin. Gastrin stimulates the production of more gastric juice.

From Bolus to Chyme

At the end of gastric digestion, food changes appearance, becoming a liquid and whitish substance called chyme.

Stomach Emptying

Chyme leaves the stomach in small jets thanks to strong contractions of the pyloric antrum (the final part of the stomach).

The pyloric sphincter opens in a controlled manner:

  • It is closed during digestion.
  • It opens periodically to let chyme pass into the duodenum.

As soon as a little chyme enters the duodenum, a reflex triggers that closes the sphincter, so the rest of the chyme waits.

This mechanism allows a slow and regulated emptying, giving the rest of the intestine time to digest properly.

Digestion in the Small Intestine and the Function of the Large Intestine

3. Intestinal Digestion

In the small intestine, nutrients are separated and prepared for absorption.

Finally, nutrients pass from the intestine into the blood and are distributed throughout the body to produce energy and make cells function.

Digestion Continues in the Small Intestine

In the stomach, food is only partially digested. The most important part of digestion takes place in the small intestine.

Here, enzymes arrive from three sources:

  • Intestine (enteric juice)
  • Pancreas (pancreatic juice)
  • Liver (bile)

All these liquids pour into the duodenum, the first section of the small intestine.

A Special Surface for Absorption

The interior of the small intestine is not smooth; it has folds, villi, and microvilli that greatly increase the surface area.

Intestinal villi are small hair-like projections, found especially in the ileum (the final section of the small intestine). There can be up to 1000 per cm².

Villi are not present in the large intestine.

What Does a Villus Contain?

  • An outer layer of epithelial cells.
  • An inner tissue with:
    • Blood vessels
    • Lymphatic vessels (called lacteals)
    • Nerve fibers
    • Contractile cells to move the villus

Enteric Juice

It is produced by the glands of the small intestine: the glands of Lieberkühn (and in the duodenum, also Brunner's glands).

Enteric juice is:

  • Alkaline: neutralizes the acidity of the chyme.
  • Rich in mucus: protects the mucosa.
  • Full of enzymes: complete digestion.

Important Enzymes in Enteric Juice

  • Enterokinase: activates trypsinogen (from the pancreas) into trypsin.
  • Endopeptidases: break down proteins within the chain.
  • Exopeptidases: break down the ends of proteins.
  • Nucleases: digest nucleic acids (DNA and RNA).
  • Enzymes on the villi: transform complex sugars:
    • Lactase: lactose → glucose + galactose
    • Maltase: maltose → glucose + glucose
    • Sucrase: sucrose → glucose + fructose

Duodenal Hormones: The Control Center of Digestion

The duodenal mucosa produces hormones that control digestion.

1. Secretin

  • Released when chyme is acidic.
  • Stimulates the pancreas to produce fluid rich in bicarbonates (to neutralize the acid).
  • Stops the production of gastric juice in the stomach: it is no longer needed!

2. Cholecystokinin-Pancreozymin (CCK)

  • Stimulates the pancreas to release digestive enzymes.
  • Causes the gallbladder to contract, so bile enters the duodenum.
  • Increases movements of the small intestine.

Pancreatic Juice

It reaches the duodenum through two channels:

  • Duct of Wirsung (main)
  • Accessory duct of Santorini

It is produced by the pancreas and contains three main enzymes:

1. Trypsinogen → Trypsin

  • Activated by enterokinase.
  • Transforms proteins and peptones into amino acids.
  • In turn, activates other pancreatic enzymes.

2. Pancreatic Amylase

  • Digests starch not yet transformed.
  • Breaks it down into disaccharides (e.g., maltose).

3. Pancreatic Lipase

  • Digests neutral fats.
  • Breaks them down into fatty acids and glycerol.

However, lipase cannot act on fats immediately; bile from the liver is needed first.

How Bile and Lipase Work Together

  1. Bile contains bile salts.
  2. Bile salts envelop fats, forming micelles.
  3. Micelles create a water-fat interface.
  4. Here, pancreatic lipase can act and break down fats.

Without bile, lipase could not properly digest fats.

Movements of the Small Intestine

The small intestine moves in a special way to mix the chyme thoroughly.

It does not push food forward continuously; it makes mixing movements called pendular movements.

These movements:

  • Lengthen and shorten small sections of the intestine.
  • Mix the chyme with digestive juices.
  • Promote contact with the villi for absorption.

The Function of the Large Intestine

The large intestine hardly digests food anymore. Its main role is to absorb water and mineral salts from the material arriving from the small intestine.

Thus, it turns the liquid into more solid feces.

Bacterial Flora: Friends Inside the Intestine

The large intestine contains billions of bacteria: this is the intestinal flora.

These bacteria:

  • Produce certain vitamins (e.g., vitamin K and some B vitamins).
  • Help digest fiber and other non-digestible substances.
  • Defend the intestine from bad bacteria.

Although useful, an excess of bacteria or the wrong kind of bacteria can cause problems.

Formation of Feces

Feces are not just leftover food. They consist of:

  • Indigestible residues (e.g., plant fiber).
  • Dead cells from the intestinal mucosa.
  • Mucus.
  • Billions of dead bacteria.

Feces are pushed toward the rectum with slow movements.

When the rectum fills up, the urge to go to the bathroom is felt.

Expulsion takes place through the anus, controlled by the anal sphincter (a muscle that opens and closes).

Bile: An Ally in Digestion

The liver continuously produces bile—about 1 liter per day.

Most of it goes into the gallbladder, where it is concentrated.

In the gallbladder:

  • Mucus is added.
  • Water and other substances are concentrated.

What Does Bile Contain?

  • Bile pigments (e.g., bilirubin, from old red blood cells)
  • Bile salts (help digest fats)
  • Water
  • Small amounts of enzymes and fats

When Does Bile Enter the Intestine?

Not always. Only during digestion. It leaves the gallbladder and enters the duodenum through the common bile duct (choledochus).

This release is stimulated by the hormone cholecystokinin-pancreozymin (CCK), produced by the duodenum when food is present.

What Is the Purpose of Bile?

  • Helps lipase digest fats (by forming micelles).
  • Neutralizes the acid of the chyme arriving from the stomach.
  • Facilitates the absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
  • Stimulates peristalsis of the intestine.
  • Protects against an excess of bacteria thanks to its antiseptic action.

From Food to Chyle

After digestion, the contents of the small intestine become a thick, white liquid called chyle.

Absorption: The Most Important Step

4. Absorption and Metabolism

Nutrients pass from the intestine into the blood and are carried throughout the body to provide energy and make organs function.

After digestion, the small intestine absorbs useful substances. This process takes place mainly in the intestinal villi.

The villi move (lengthening and shortening) to allow substances to pass into blood and lymphatic vessels.

What Does the Intestine Absorb?

Into the blood (via the capillaries of the villi) go:

  • Amino acids (from proteins)
  • Monosaccharides (e.g., glucose from sugars)
  • Glycerol (from certain fats)
  • Water-soluble vitamins (B complex, C)
  • Water and mineral salts

These substances enter the mesenteric veins, which then form the hepatic portal vein, taking everything directly to the liver.

The liver:

  • Checks the absorbed substances.
  • Filters them.
  • Regulates their quantity.
  • Stores some of them.

After the liver, the blood passes into the hepatic veins, then into the inferior vena cava, and returns to the general circulation.

Into the Lymphatic Vessels (Lacteals)

They mainly absorb:

  • Fatty acids
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)

These substances enter the lymphatic vessels of the villi (called lacteals).

Then:

  1. They go to the cisterna chyli (in the abdomen).
  2. They pass into the thoracic duct.
  3. The thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein.
  4. From here they enter the blood.

From the Small to the Large Intestine

As useful substances are absorbed, the intestinal content loses fluids and becomes denser.

Peristalsis pushes it toward the large intestine.

In the Large Intestine: No Digestion, Lots of Transformation

In the large intestine there are no enzymes, so no digestion takes place.

However, other important things happen:

  • Absorption of water and mineral salts: the material becomes increasingly solid.
  • Action of bacteria: they ferment certain fibers and produce gas and vitamins.
  • Formation of feces: indigestible residues, dead cells, mucus, and bacteria accumulate.

Thanks to water absorption, the material becomes progressively denser and turns into feces.

Movements in the Large Intestine

The large intestine moves slowly. Occasionally, it makes strong contractions called mass movements (massive peristalsis). These push feces toward the rectum.

Expulsion of Feces

When the rectum fills up, the body feels the urge to go to the bathroom.

Expulsion is controlled by the anal sphincter: a muscle that can open and close voluntarily.

Under normal conditions, feces are expelled once or twice a day, but everyone is different.

The Liver

The liver is not just for producing bile; that is just one of its many functions. In reality, it is a large laboratory of the body.

It weighs about 1,500 grams and is located in the upper right part of the abdomen.

It receives:

  • Substances absorbed by the intestine, via the hepatic portal vein.
  • Waste products produced by body cells.

Main Functions of the Liver

  1. Produces essential amino acids: used to build cell and blood proteins.
  2. Synthesizes albumins: important blood plasma proteins.
  3. Synthesizes globulins: help with blood clotting and the immune system.
  4. Converts glucose into glycogen: stores it as an energy reserve.
  5. Manages sugars and fats: regulates glucose and lipid metabolism.
  6. Neutralizes toxic substances: such as alcohol, medications, or body waste.
  7. Produces cholesterol, bile acids, and bilirubin: the main components of bile.

Metabolism

Metabolism is the set of chemical reactions that allow the body to live, grow, and produce energy.

Two Main Phases

  • Anabolic phase (constructive): the body transforms food into energy or new matter. Also called assimilation.
  • Catabolic phase (destructive): the body breaks down used substances. Waste products exit via urine, sweat, and carbon dioxide.

Metabolic Balance

  • In youth: the anabolic phase prevails → growth occurs.
  • In adulthood: the two phases are in equilibrium.
  • In old age: the catabolic phase prevails → mass and tissues are lost.

Enzymes and Body Conditions

Metabolism depends on thousands of enzymes (ferments). There are about 25,000, and many more are yet to be discovered.

Enzymes only work if:

  • The environment has the correct acidity.
  • Catalysts (such as mineral salts or vitamins) are present.
  • The temperature is correct.

Many of these reactions cannot be reproduced in a laboratory. For example, the complete synthesis of very long proteins has only been partially achieved, and with the help of artificial systems.

Homeostasis: The Body's Balance

Normal metabolism keeps the body's internal conditions stable. This balance is called homeostasis.

It includes:

  • Composition of fluids (blood, lymph).
  • Body temperature.
  • Sugar and mineral salt levels.

Basal Metabolism

It is the minimum amount of energy the body uses when completely at rest.

It is needed for essential functions such as:

  • Maintaining temperature.
  • Making the heart beat.
  • Breathing.
  • Producing chemical substances.

Basal metabolism corresponds to cellular respiration.

How Is It Measured?

A special device is used to measure oxygen consumption.

Then, through calculations that take into account:

  • Age
  • Weight
  • Height
  • Body surface area

the daily energy requirement is estimated.

The Thyroid Regulates Metabolism

The thyroid gland influences the metabolism of all cells. If it produces too many hormones, metabolism accelerates; if it produces too few, it slows down.
